truth_boundary: Measured parameter sweeps of the existing kinematic ride-quality screen (scripts/simulate_smooth_stair_climb.py), run by varying one input at a time and recording the reported result. Not FEA, not dynamic contact simulation, not a physical test. Every row was produced by actually running the screen, not by interpolation or closed-form estimate.
purpose: The ride_quality gate has failed since the wheel was grown to 430 mm, and the previously chosen remedy -- sourcing a faster corner actuator -- was shown by audit_power_budget.py's ride_quality_actuator_power_crosscheck to be electrically infeasible with the sourced pack. This file records what the two remaining physical levers actually buy, so the design fork is decided against measured numbers rather than intuition, and so these sweeps are not re-derived later.
method_SRC: scripts/simulate_smooth_stair_climb.py run repeatedly with a single input patched per run; data/te_v059_parameters.json and data/te_v059_load_cases.json restored byte-identical afterwards. Ride-quality result, chassis ramp-tracking error, and the searched required actuator velocity were read from the screen's own JSON output.

minimum_combined_climb_forward_speed_mps.enforcement: HARD -- scripts/audit_design_acceptance.py raises SystemExit(1) below this value
minimum_combined_climb_forward_speed_mps.traces_to: Master requirement that the stroller must not break stride or wait at the stair edge.

chassis_ramp_error_budget_mm_ASSUMED.enforcement: SOFT -- honest FAIL, does not block the build
chassis_ramp_error_budget_mm_ASSUMED.note: Self-documented in its own reason field as an engineering target, NOT a sourced ride-comfort standard. This is the only one of the three colliding constraints that is not either sourced hardware or a locked master requirement.

pack_max_continuous_discharge_A_SRC.enforcement: Physical limit of the sourced cells

lever_1_wheel_diameter.description: Wheel diameter swept at the mandated 0.2 m/s forward speed. A larger wheel bridges the stair nosing on a flatter natural rolling path, so less residual is left for the corner actuator to cancel.
lever_1_wheel_diameter.finding: Growing the wheel genuinely helps, and helps twice over: chassis ramp error falls monotonically (86.1 mm to 25.5 mm) AND the required actuator power falls by 8x (1455 W to 181 W per corner), which would also dissolve the battery conflict. But the budget is still not met at 900 mm, and a 900 mm wheel exceeds the 750 mm overall_width_gate_mm and is taller than the stroller's own packaging envelope. This lever cannot close the gate within anything that remains a stroller.
lever_1_wheel_diameter.closes_at_ASSUMED: Extrapolating the trend, roughly 910-930 mm would meet the 25 mm budget. Not swept further because the result is already outside the packaging gate and therefore moot.

lever_2_forward_speed.description: Forward speed swept at the current 430 mm wheel. Slowing the climb gives the actuator more time per stair, so a tighter (better-tracking) smoothing window becomes reachable within the actuator's rated speed.
lever_2_forward_speed.rows_note: The sweep also ran 0.15, 0.12, 0.10, 0.08, 0.07 and 0.06 m/s. Those runs completed and were consistent with the monotonic trend shown, but their detailed output was not retained, so they are deliberately omitted rather than reconstructed from memory. Every row listed above is a directly recorded measurement.
lever_2_forward_speed.finding: Slowing down helps but cannot close the gate either. At 0.031 m/s -- already 6.5x below the HARD 0.2 m/s acceptance floor -- chassis ramp error is still 31.3 mm against the 25 mm budget. This lever is therefore blocked twice: by the locked no-break-stride requirement, and on its own physics even if that requirement were waived.
lever_2_forward_speed.note_on_speed_shortfall_factor: speed_shortfall_factor compares the required velocity against the actuator's FULL rated speed (170.5 mm/s), while the screen's own window selection derates that by actuator_speed_margin_fraction_ASSUMED = 0.8 (136.4 mm/s). That is why the 0.031 m/s row can show a shortfall below 1.0 while ride_quality still FAILs: the window that would meet the budget needs 166.1 mm/s, which fits inside the raw rating but not inside the design's own safety margin. Reported here so the apparent contradiction is not mistaken for a bug.

lever_3_faster_actuator.description: The remedy previously chosen. Not swept here because it is settled elsewhere.
lever_3_faster_actuator.why: Two independent blocks. (1) Component availability: no compact BLDC family reaches the required torque x speed product; Dunkermotoren BG75 dMove (all stacks) and maxon EC 90 flat were checked against real datasheets and are 2.8x and 3.6x short respectively -- see data/te_v059_physics_elements.json reselection_candidates_checked_SRC. (2) Electrical feasibility: even granting a hypothetical actuator that delivers it, powering four of them exceeds the sourced pack. At a physically impossible 100% efficiency, ignoring wheel drives, pod actuators and electronics entirely, the corner actuators alone draw 90.95 A against the pack's 90 A continuous rating, and give 4.32 min runtime against a 5 min target. See scripts/audit_power_budget.py ride_quality_actuator_power_crosscheck. Because that figure is a lower bound, no efficiency or duty-cycle argument recovers it.

lever_4_relax_the_ramp_error_budget.description: The 25 mm budget was the only one of the three colliding constraints that was neither sourced hardware nor a locked master requirement, so it was the obvious candidate to relax. Checked against the real standard rather than adjusted to force a pass.
lever_4_relax_the_ramp_error_budget.standard_SRC: ISO 2631-1:1997 comfort reaction bands; see data/te_v059_load_cases.json chassis_ramp_error_budget_iso_2631_check for the bands, the source-confidence caveat, and the conversion method.
lever_4_relax_the_ramp_error_budget.finding: The 25 mm budget converts to 0.358 m/s^2 unweighted RMS at the stair-passing frequency -- essentially the ISO 2631-1 'not uncomfortable' ceiling of 0.315 m/s^2, and below it once Wk attenuation is applied. Far from being a soft number chosen for convenience, it turns out to be well-calibrated. The achieved 86.1 mm converts to 1.232 m/s^2, in the 'uncomfortable' band, for a child occupant. The 3.44x ratio between them is independent of the Wk weighting factor, so this conclusion does not depend on the one value that could not be verified from a primary source.
lever_4_relax_the_ramp_error_budget.consequence: Relaxing the budget cannot be justified against the real standard, so the fourth and last lever is closed too. The over-constraint is genuine and must be resolved by changing the architecture, not by adjusting a number.

conclusion.statement: The design is over-constrained. Three constraints collide and no two-of-three can be satisfied while the third holds: forward speed >= 0.2 m/s (locked master requirement), chassis ramp error <= 25 mm (unsourced engineering target), and the sourced 90 A / 314.5 Wh battery pack. All three physical levers that could relieve the collision have now been measured and exhausted -- a faster actuator is electrically infeasible, a slower climb is blocked by a locked requirement and fails anyway, and a larger wheel needs ~900 mm against a 750 mm packaging gate.
conclusion.consequence: Closing ride_quality requires changing the corner mechanism so that required actuator power stops scaling with the full static corner load, or moving the comfort duty off the chassis entirely. It is not a component-selection problem and should not be pursued as one.
conclusion.budget_relaxation_ruled_out: The obvious escape -- relaxing the unsourced 25 mm budget -- was checked against ISO 2631-1 and closed: 25 mm sits essentially on the 'not uncomfortable' ceiling, and the achieved 86.1 mm falls in the 'uncomfortable' band. See lever_4_relax_the_ramp_error_budget. The standard was looked up to find out what it said, and it happened to confirm the budget rather than rescue the design.
conclusion.OPEN: Which architectural change to make is a design decision with no objectively-correct answer and is NOT made here. Two candidates have been identified but neither has been analysed: (1) carry the 1324 N static corner load on a spring or gas strut so the actuator supplies only the dynamic delta, which is how high-bandwidth active suspensions keep power down -- required power would stop scaling with the full static load; (2) move vertical isolation to the occupant pod, which carries only ~35 kg (343 N) against the corner's 1324 N and already has an actuated pitch joint, so isolating the child needs far less force, stroke and power than levelling the whole chassis. Option (2) also arguably serves the real requirement -- occupant comfort -- more directly than chassis ramp tracking does.
